Artemis. The goddess of the hunt, wild animals, and the moon in Greek mythology, also known as Diana to the Romans. She is the twin sister of Apollo, born on the island of Delos alongside him. Artemis is one of the twelve Olympian deities, venerated as a virgin goddess who fiercely protects her independence and that of her followers.

Artemis and Apollo were fraternal twins born to Zeus and Leto on Delos, which became a major religious center honoring both deities. She is typically depicted as a young woman with a bow and arrow, accompanied by a deer or hounds. Her domain encompasses wilderness, hunting, and the protection of wild animals, making her a paradoxical figure who embodies both the violence of the hunt and the nurture of nature's creatures. She was the sworn virgin goddess who famously rejected all suitors and requests for marriage, asking her father Zeus to grant her eternal virginity and a band of virgin attendants, sometimes called the Amazons or nymphs. Yet despite being always virginal herself, she also serves as protector of young women and childbirth. Girls entering adulthood were initiated into her cult, and she was invoked during labor.

Artemis was venerated across Greece but had particularly important sanctuaries at Delos, her birthplace, and at Ephesus in Anatolia, where the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. She is fiercely protective of her virginity and that of her followers, punishing those who transgress against her most famously by transforming the hunter Actaeon into a stag after he glimpsed her bathing. The moon is her celestial realm, and she drives her silver chariot across the night sky. She is often conflated with Selene, the personified moon goddess, and later with Hecate, the goddess of magic and the crossroads. She shares a father with Apollo and with many other divine and heroic figures throughout Greek mythology.
